fatal_errors: The proposed material is not the equimolar WTaTiVZr alloy studied in the target; no definite replacement-alloy composition is specified.
The intervention removes W and Ta, whereas the target deliberately incorporates both in an arc-melted WTaTiVZr alloy.
The baseline is incorrectly described as a tungsten-rich HEA rather than commercially sourced powder-sintered pure tungsten.
The response predicts activation and irradiation performance under reactor conditions even though these properties were not measured in the target study.

The cited evidence establishes general fusion-material requirements and tungsten limitations but does not demonstrate that the proposed substitutions preserve strength, irradiation resistance, or BCC phase stability.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the broad need for low-activation, high-temperature fusion-facing materials, but it does not reconstruct the reported material or study. The target concerns an as-cast equimolar WTaTiVZr two-BCC-phase alloy tested against pure tungsten through compression, indentation from room temperature to 500 °C, and scratch toughness measurements. Its reported advantages were higher strength, improved plasticity, a lower apparent brittle-to-ductile transition range, and approximately 52% greater scratch-derived fracture toughness. The generated hypothesis instead proposes an unspecified W/Ta/Mo-free alloy and focuses on unmeasured neutron activation and irradiation behavior at temperatures above 1000 K. Its proposed comparative irradiation experiment is reasonably falsifiable, but the preservation of mechanical and radiation properties is not supported by the cited excerpts, so it is not a well-supported alternative.
